title: Your House Is Not a Hotel
author: J. Chase Davis
summary: J. Chase Davis summarizes the argument of Adam Madden's book The Productive Household: most Christian families fail at family worship not from laziness but because they are never in the same room. The modern household, he says, has dad, mom and children each productive and formed elsewhere, with the few shared hours given to recreation. Madden recalls a survey of a hundred teenagers in a conservative church where fewer than ten percent read the Bible or prayed with family even monthly, which Davis treats as a scheduling problem rather than a piety problem. Madden refuses both the option of grinding harder inside the same arrangement and the option of fleeing to a farm, asking instead what one step toward more time together might be. His own story of buying a dog boarding business and then smoking trout shows the doors are more open than men assume. Davis insists the businesses are downstream: a family-integrated business only buys context, and the real work inside it is worship, instruction, correction and a present, imitable father.
points: Davis argues that families fail at family worship mainly because the household schedule keeps everyone apart, not because parents are lazy or unbelieving.

Madden rejects both grinding harder inside the same arrangement and the eject button of selling everything for acreage, asking instead for one step toward being together more.
His family built a dog boarding business and a trout operation with no capital, showing that opportunities are more open than most men assume.
A family business is only a tool that buys context; the actual work is worship, instruction, correction and a father present enough to be imitated.
quotes: Most Christian families are not failing at family worship because they’re lazy. They’re failing because they’re never in the same room.
Everyone sleeps under the same roof and spends ninety-five percent of their waking hours apart, and the few hours that are left get spent on recreation.
Those parents believed the right things. They worked separately, ran to ball games, and got home at nine.
He is telling men to ask a different question: how do I take one step toward being with my family more instead of less, and what could we build together once we’re there?
A family-integrated business is a tool. It buys you context. What you put into that context is the actual work.
The work is worship, instruction, correction, a father who is present enough to be imitated.
You can buy the business. You can get the land. And your children will want nothing to do with any of it, because they don’t know you and they don’t like being around you.
